PARANOID MANIFESTATIONS ARE WIDESPREAD, and represent some of the distortions of personality of most people. Throughout this paper, which is concerned with paranoid psychodynamics, whenever a reference is made to "the paranoid, " the designation refers to any form or degree of paranoid activity.

The original article commenced with that paragraph, but inasmuch as it was presented twenty-five years ago and appeared in a short-lived, relatively obscure journal, its modified republication calls for comment on developments concerning concepts of "paranoia" during the intervening period.

In the mid-fifties the basic views regarding paranoid conditions were derivative of Freud's constructs (1911) as worked out in his study of Schreber's autobiographical material (1903). Paranoid disturbance was regarded essentially as engendered by latent homosexuality defended against by delusions of persecution and grandeur. Diagnostic criteria rested heavily on suspiciousness, ideas of reference and especially delusions of persecution.

Regarding the term "paranoia, " Colby (1975) affirms that "Little agreement about the meaning of the term 'paranoia' was reached until this half of the present century, when it received solid adjectival status, as 'paranoid personality' and 'paranoid state.'" Freedman and Schwab (1978) discuss, however, significant distortions of diagnosis and treatment deriving from occurrence of paranoid symptoms in a multiplicity of mental disorders. In spite, therefore, of its "solid adjectival status, " the attribution does not clarify the (nonorganic) clinical conditions wherein it occurs. Reply to Dr. Meissner

Walter Bonime M.D.

Walter Bonime

Walter Bonime, M.D.
10 Park Avenue
New York, New York 10016

Walter Bonime  

THE PUBLICATION OF MEISSNER'S volume, The Paranoid Process(1978), was welcome and promised much by its title alone. The title emphasized the importance of process, implicit also in the term, "psychodynamics." Additionally welcome was the extensive clinical material—three hundred pages devoted to careful, intensive study of just ten cases; detailed clinical presentation in the best tradition of Freud's introduction of psychoanalytic concepts.

There is, therefore, a basis for some fundamental agreement in our dealing with the problems of paranoia. We stress in our presentations focusing on concrete individual cases, and we both emphasize process. Despite parallelism in some fundamental views, we also, almost paradoxically, differ: I speak as a culturalist, and Meissner accounts for identical individual behaviors quite otherwise, because his thinking is in terms of classical Freudian concepts. At the outset, he disqualifies psychodynamics from the purview of process. He considers my concepts as something that "hovers in the background of the reflection of paranoid psychodynamics, [remaining] … unfocused and nonspecific…" He says, "I will not pursue the dimension of process … since it would carry us too far afield…" But, to explain the clinical phenomena in my last and major case, he nevertheless invokes "the schema suggested by the paranoid process…" We obviously have different views of process and psychodynamics. For me, Meissner's concepts of paranoid process represent his particular analysis of paranoid psychodynamics. I have different concepts of the pathological process which I refer to directly as paranoid psychodynamics. Despite this semantic difference, we recognize certain important phenomena in essentially identical ways.

One of the most crucial points of agreement, for example, that we have in our observations is the fact that the paranoid frequently functions in such ways as to elicit from others the very behavior he experiences as hostile and persecutory. This is a focal point in my discussion of "projection"; it is correspondingly stated and illustrated in Meissner's book (e.g., Gloria, p. 330; Bob, p. 207).

Gilead Nachmani  

I WOULD LIKE TO REVIEW first some of Dr. Grotstein's basic formulations and definitions and then relate them to several implications of the negative therapeutic reaction from the perspective of interpersonal and developmental theory.

The model of the mind is intrapsychic and endopsychic, and it is pre-interpersonal, although implicit is a receptiveness to human relatedness in an external reality which is interpersonal. Early infantile fantasies, the prototypes of yet undeveloped organizing principles, are introjected and become internal objects. Some of these fantasies, particularly those attached to experiences of greed, envy, and the belief that undifferentiated objects upon which the infant is quite dependent can be destroyed and recreated, are not relinquished. These fantasies constitute the principle ingredients of a bad-self conception. For reasons that are intrapsychic, and not interpersonal, the infant does not emerge from a paranoid-schizoid position onto the threshold of the depressive position, and subsequently experiences an almost chronic paranoid anxiety with beliefs of being possessed, controlled, and in a pact with the Devil. Most threatening to these people is the emergence of consciousness insofar as it brings about the possibility of acknowledging dependency and the relinquishing of omnipotent fantasies about creation and destruction. One can speculate that idealizations are tenaciously retained because they cannot contain the pain of disillusionment while separating and individuating from the object upon whom they depend. The internal objects, the unconscious fantasies, seemingly made a pact in order to obtain a moment of nonexistence, of obliviousness to dependency and the pain of human relatedness, and the person continues to live in a morbidly psychotic fantasy world in which he continues to 'create' gods and devils of his underworld to explain his bitter existence.

What emerges from this mental process is a person who spends much time living out self-negation. Among the forms which this takes are negative therapeutic reactions and beliefs that they are humanly inaccessible and impossible to help; that is, they are unanalyzable. They do not seem to learn from experience.

Moral Courage and the Regeneration of Hope

Edward Ericson

Edward Ericson

Edward L. Ericson
2 West 64th Street
New York, N.Y. 10023

Edward Ericson  

IN THE LITERATURE OF PSYCHOLOGY and religious biography it is commonly recognized that human beings can survive enormous hardships and handicaps as long as they have hope. But people disintegrate and even die, without other apparent causes, if they are deprived of hope. All of us have experienced in some measure the effects of hope and despair and know the ravages of profound hopelessness upon the lives of close friends and relatives—if we have not undergone such crises ourselves. Probably few families are spared the experience of acute despondency striking some member like a ravenous cancer.

What is true for the individual is also true for the group. But hope and despair are highly contagious, sweeping at times as social storms over whole populations and civilizations. The psychology of mass hysteria operates by its own laws and rhythms when the defenses of individual judgment and discrimination are down. Periodically civilization has suffered its dark hours of collective desperation and moral insanity when crimes have been committed by those presumed to be the best of people for allegedly the finest of causes. More frequently, the opportunity to make a better life for ourselves and others is allowed to pass without recognition, or at least without decisive action, because we believe ourselves impotent to change our lives or to effect history.

When we are down, we are told to cheer up—usually with the effect of making us feel worse. When we are defeated, we are urged to try, try, again, to struggle harder against our sense of exhaustion. We praise courage and recommend it to those who are fearful or anxious, but like the Cowardly Lion in the Wizard of Oz, we are not always able to locate the courage we require.

Countertransference and Parataxis

Alan Grey Ph.D.

Alan Grey

Alan L. Grey, Ph.D.
103 East 86th Street
New York, New York 10028

Alan Grey  

EVEN THOSE MOST DEDICATED to the search for knowledge sometimes are dismayed by what they find. A noteworthy instance was Freud's initial report (1910) of the phenomenon he called "countertransference". Early references to it reflect that the idiosyncratic reactions of the analyst were a source of considerable dismay. A fault had been uncovered in the most fundamental strata of psychoanalysis, unreliability in the very evidence on which it is based. How to sort out the pure gold mined from the patient's unconscious from the contaminating leaks of the therapist? In short, the initial assessment saw "countertransference" as a grave, even disqualifying flaw in the analyst.

That view proved unduly pessimistic and was, in the course of time, revised. Certain of its conceptual sources, however, lie so deep within the theoretical structure of classical psychoanalysis that vestiges of that negative attitude persist to this day. Such preconceptions only add to the difficulties of analysts in dealing with themselves, so they are best laid to rest. Toward that goal, it becomes useful to expose some implicit premises in which the classical idea of countertransference are rooted. The sketchiest of reminders can suffice for present purposes. One of them is to recall that "countertransference errors" originally were understood to be psychopathological in origin and not as providing useful information. Thus they were grossly inappropriate to the analyst's function in the treatment process.

The obvious solution was to eliminate such occurrences by requiring candidates to undergo training analysis, but it was at least a decade after 1910 until the training analysis became mandatory. Put another way, it took that long before countertransference was acknowledged to occur in the work of all candidates. And it took even longer for general acceptance of the fact that even successful training analysis does not eliminate such subjective reactions. Happily, another discovery came along to temper these discouragements.

Sullivan's Concept of the Illusory Other—Sullivan's the Illusory Other

Jarl Dyrud M.D.

Jarl Dyrud

Jarl Dyrud, M.D.
Biological Sciences Division University of Chicago
Chicago, Illinois 60637

Jarl Dyrud  

"THE ILLUSORY OTHER" IS AN attractive term because it suggests at once the inappropriateness of my version of you to what is in fact transpiring between us. Yet it could mislead us in two ways. (1) According to interpersonal theory, it should not stand alone, and (2) the term "illusory" implies that, being a fabrication of the mind, it should be gotten rid of so that something more "real" can take its place. I mention these potential misinterpretations because our common language is still the language of individual psychology. We are prone as was Sullivan to slip into speaking of parataxic distortions as if they were one-way processes rather than speaking of a parataxic dyad. Nevertheless, Sullivan chose to wrestle with the grammar of subject and object in order to go the more rigorous way of trying to apply the philosophy of social behaviorism to the clinical practice of psychiatry.

In his lecture The Data of Psychiatry(1938) Sullivan made it clear that the illusory other is part of a dyad made up as much of my version of myself as it is of my version of the other person. This envelope seems to reduce my anxiety by providing a framework of expectations within which I can be comfortable.

Parenthood as a Developmental Phase

DURING THE LAST TWO DECADES—especially with the impetus of Erikson's conceptions of the life cycle—there has been a growing awareness in the psychoanalytic and developmental literature of parenthood as a developmental phase. Our understanding of the development of parental attitudes and tasks does not match in its refinement the careful stage-distinctions we have made for the child's development. In part this is understandable since parenthood usually occurs in adult life when the rate of change in personality has slowed down and has become relatively stable and, in varying degree, resistant to modification. However, on more detailed observations of parent-child interactions it becomes apparent that there are frequent and important fluctuations of parental attitudes that occur in interaction with the child's rapid development. The particular parental task at a given stage of the child's development is defined in part by the particular social and family group, in part by the idiosyncratic personal character of the parents—including their expectations, idealizations and sensitivities—and in part by the actual developmental experiences of the child which are sometimes most operationally described in terms of the child's behavioral impact on parental behavior.

DURING THE COURSE OF TREATING2 severely or predominantly obsessional people, and of helping other therapists treat them, I have observed some phenomena that have prompted me to reconsider aspects of the classic psychoanalytic model of obsessionalism. In the three patients whose treatment will be delineated here, consistent early developmental factors provided clues to a modified conceptualization of obsessional structure. I believe that this hypothesis concerning the dynamics of obsessional functioning points to ways in which the therapeutic usefulness of the psychoanalytic model can be expanded.

The obsessional patient is often experienced by therapists as particularly irritating. In addition, sometimes the newer therapist—and even the more experienced therapist—finds it difficult to remember that the obsessional's doubting, labyrinthian logic, and apparent lack of movement are not a reflection of insufficient skills in the therapist. I believe that the distance provided by the theory of obsessional development to be presented here may also help the therapist to deal with some of the special problems presented by these patients.

Among my obsessional patients I noted certain similarities of background, especially in what I call the parental style. Although there were variations, each patient had at least one harshly critical parent. The criticism started early in life and had a flailing, arbitrary ring to it from which the child could not escape. The parent's comments usually began with physical appearance, such as: "Your mouth is too small, " "Your nose is too large, " "Your hair is awful."

Sullivan and Fromm11

Clara Thompson M.D.

Clara Thompson

Clara Thompson, M.D.
20 West 74th Street
New York, New York 10023

Clara Thompson  

IN THE LATE 1920'S, PSYCHOANALYSTS began to concern themselves with character analysis, and a few years later some analysts became interested in the study of comparative cultures and in the application of the findings of modern anthropology to the study of the development of human personality. Fromm and Sullivan became outstanding contributors in both of these fields, and each has his own unique contribution to the subjects.

Fromm is a social psychologist, trained in the classical Freudian school of psychoanalysis, while Sullivan was a psychiatrist with a background in American psychiatry under William Alanson White and Adolf Meyer. Although well-versed in the theories and practices of psychoanalysis, Sullivan did not have direct contact with any of the European schools of analysis. About 1934, Sullivan and Fromm met for the first time, and for several years thereafter there was working collaboration between them at the Washington School of Psychiatry and the William Alanson White Institute. They held certain concepts in common, but each preserved his own particular approach to the problems. The work of each supplements the other, and their basic assumptions about human beings are similar. The chief area which they share in common is the interest in the impact of cultural pressures on personality development. The chief area of difference is in theories about the self.

Early in his career as a psychiatrist, Sullivan became interested in what goes on between people, especially in the areas of interaction, which seemed to create difficulties in living. This early interest, growing out of clinical observation, became further stimulated and its scope enlarged through his growing interest in the findings of cultural anthropology, especially as demonstrated in the work of Ruth Benedict and Edward Sapir.

The other idiosyncrasy of the philosophers is no less dangerous; it consists in confusing the last and the first. They place that which comes at the end—unfortunately! for it ought not to come at all!—namely, the 'highest concepts.' which means the most general, the emptiest concepts, the last smoke of evaporating reality, in the beginning, as the beginning. This again is nothing but their way of showing reverence: the higher may not grow out of the lower, may not have grown at all.
Nietzsche (from Twilight of the Idols)

ONE OF THE LIVELIEST AND MOST CONTROVERSIAL areas in psychoanalytic theorizing over the past two decades has been in the attempt of various writers to adapt classical drive theory to the clinical phenomena and conceptual problems posed by the more severe characterological disturbances. Heinz Kohut's contributions have been among the most fertile and stimulating in this area. His earlier work, although clearly introducing novel theoretical perspectives, was largely focused on issues of psychoanalytic technique. The Analysis of the Self, published in 1971, delineated "narcissistic personality disorders" as a diagnostic concept with a specific developmental origin, demanding a new treatment approach; Kohut introduced major technical innovations designed to deal with the unique transference phenomena which, he argued, emerged in the analytic treatment of this group of patients. IN THIS PRESENTATION, I WISH to delineate what I see as Erich Fromm's radical contribution to understanding man—the human animal who, by the nature of his existence, must make decisions and the choice whether to be genuinely alive or to stagnate. By combining a clinical wisdom secured through almost 50 years of intensive psychoanalytic experience with a life-long devotion to humanistic studies, Fromm (1947) has fashioned a conceptual formulation of man's nature which is unique and classical in its vigor and simplicity.

The major thrust of Fromm's theoretical view of man is that man must transform his life experience to bring himself into life—that adaptive modifications of personality are, in truth, not sufficient to accomplish this serious task. Although not clearly acknowledged, man's search for relatedness and identity comprises the bed-rock of human existence. The biological condition of man provides inadequate instinctive determination for this search. The evolutionary emergence of the specifically human phenomenon, self-awareness, forces on man an awesome sense of separateness. Man is inescapably compelled to find a solution to the central question posed by life—that is, how to transcend his separateness and relate himself to his world. Fromm delineates two contrasting modes of relatedness: regression to earlier and often archaic forms of relatedness, or to hope-oriented, affirmative responses in the direction of becoming fully human through developing one's creativity, productivity, and ability to love. Each of us has the potential for the most archaic as well as the most progressive solutions.

PSYCHOANALYSIS IS, IN VERY LARGE measure, the sustained and disciplined effort to overcome or to remove the obstacles that stand in the way of open, direct communication with the people and the world around us.1 The capacity to communicate is, of course, one of the greatest traditional themes of literature. Dostoievsky's Prince Mishkin and his Alyosha Karamazov, for example, had an almost uncanny ability to establish immediate and intimate contact with people. True encounter and communication arouse and energize the soul.

IN THIS PAPER3 I SHALL PRESENT a synthesis of the ideas which I have developed in various articles and books regarding the concept of "projective counteridentification". I first coined this term in 1957 to refer to a specific and differential aspect of countertransference, based on the unconscious analytic interaction between the patient and the analyst, and which is brought about by the particularly intense use of and psychopathic modality of the mechanism of projective identification of the patient. As a result of the pathological quality of this mechanism, the patient is able to induce different roles, affects and fantasies in the analyst, who unconsciously and passively feels himself "carried along" to play and experience them. I should like to refer briefly to the mechanism of projective identification.

This was described by Melanie Klein in her paper "Some Notes on Schizoid Mechanisms" (1946), and included in her hypotheses about emotional development in the first months of life. The Literature

The Dearth of Literature

A MOST SIGNIFICANT FEATURE in the area of countertransference towards children and adolescents is the limited literature. Of 217 references on countertransference provided by an American Psychology Association Abstract Search covering 1967 to 1976, only 10 references—six of which were foreign sources—pertained to children or adolescents. The Bibliography for Training in Child Psychiatry(Berlin, 1976) has 19 references. The venerable Psychoanalytic Study of the Child provides 10 index entries in 25 years. The three editions of the Index of Psychoanalytic Writings cite only 17 references from 1900 to 1969. A scan of subject indexes in child therapy books reveals only nominal attention to countertransference.

Several authors also have noted the relative lack of attention to countertransference. Maurice Green (1972) speaks of the "neglect, " as does Christ (1964) and Akaret and Stockhamer (1965) with respect to late adolescents.

Similarly, in case conferences and reports, attention has traditionally been on topics other than the therapist's feelings.

DR. NACHMANI'S DISCUSSION CONSTITUTES what I believe to be a complementarity in its own right to the formulations I am employing. Fundamentally, I believe that all psychological phenomena have to be seen from a dual-track principle, not unlike the double helix of the gene, which contains the disparate strands emerging from a common vertex. This common vertex is designated by Bion mathematically as the "O" of the experience itself ("at-one-ment"). Our transformations of "O" into "K" (knowledge about the experience) occupies two tracks, the sensual (externally real) and intuitive (internally real), corresponding to the bilaterality of the data-processing of the cerebral hemispheres, the sense organs, etc. Thus, from the psychoanalytic point(s) of view, we must consider experience ("O") as having two transformations in "K", one the realistic "impingement" of the external world upon our senses and the other the preconceptions, inherent and acquired (the inherent instinctual organization) which subjectively "greet" this data according to its phylogenetically-honed programming. This "greeting" of the data by the subjective, holistic, right brain organization is in the preliterate form of narrative known as phantasy.

Psychoanalytically, we must explain "O" from the vertices of internal and external reality. When we are able to "binocularize" both these points of view, we have conducted a mind expansion via interpretation of a transformation of "K" into "O", the realization of the significance of the experience. To the Editor:

Following a discussion with Donald Meltzer, I have thought through some issues with regard to my paper, "Who is the Dreamer Who Dreams the Dream and Who is the Dreamer Who Understands It?", Contemporary Psychoanalysis, 15 1, 1979. I especially wish to expand on Bion's conception of alpha function and should desire to add the following to my discussion of that important theme.

On Alpha Function

IT IS TO BION'S ALPHA FUNCTION that we must look for the ultimate, irreducible element of creativity for it unites the Dreamer Who Dreams the Dream, the Dreamer Who Understands the Dream, the Dreamer Who Makes the Dream Understandable etc. (Bion, 1962, 1963, 1965, 1970). Bion believes that alpha function, which corresponds to Freud's primary process but is more extensive, processes the data of experience (beta elements) which confront the sense organs and cause them to undergo an "alpha-betization" in order to become capable of mental digestion as elements of thought. This "alpha-betization" also accounts for the transformation of the sense-ible experience into sensual imagery (via image-ination) which then qualify as dream images which can be dreamed and stored. It is my impression that the transformations of the sense impression into imagery are facilitated by alpha function's access to inherent and acquired preconceptions, that is, to archetypes, which are always pressuring to surface but require a sense-ible experience for a vehicle.

Ernest Wolf M.D.

Ernest Wolf

Ernest S. Wolf, M.D.
1333 Tower Rd.

Ernest Wolf  

I

IN HIS ADDRESS TO THE Nuremberg Psychoanalytic Congress, Freud (1910) for the first time took note of countertransference, and described it as arising in the physician as a result of the influence of the patient on the physician's unconscious feelings. In subsequent years countertransference has been widely discussed in the psychoanalytic literature, and there have been a number of excellent surveys of the topic. Gradually, and especially in recent years, there has been a shift in emphasis away from seeing countertransference primarily as an undesirable interference in the analytic process emanating from the psychoanalyst. Attention has been increasingly called to the uses of countertransference as a diagnostic and therapeutic tool in the conduct of psychoanalytic treatment. Such shifts are characteristic of the development of psychoanalytic science, and they herald significant advances in psychoanalytic treatment and in psychoanalytic theory. Typically, what at first appears to be an obstacle in the path of psychoanalysis is transformed into one of the tools that facilitates the psychoanalytic process. Clinical experience, combined with novel theoretical conceptualizations, allows these transformations to occur. Thus, Freud turned the difficulties attending investigations in a hypnotic trance and the resistances to suggestions into the technique of free association.

IN THIS PAPER THERE IS NO intention to offer a complete review of the literature on the topic of countertransference. Langs (1976) has already published comprehensive and scholarly chapters, which review the literature on countertransference from the time of Freud's earliest statement on the phenomenon (Freud 1910), to the significant papers published as late as 1976. We are interested here in tracing the development of the key themes and issues from their inception to their current status in contemporary psychoanalytic thinking.

One must start with a recognition of the incisiveness of Freud's thought. His earliest remarks on the identification of countertransference, in that famous paragraph whose second sentence begins with, "We have become aware of the 'countertransference' which arises [in the physician] as a result of the patient's influence on his unconscious feelings …", also contains the phrase "he shall begin his activity with a self-analysis and continually carry it deeper while he is making his observations on his patients" (Freud 1910). Otto Will  

Introduction

IN THESE COMMENTS I shall refer briefly to some aspects of the professional life of the psychotherapist that may become so intertwined with his personal life that occasionally may seem to become indistinguishable from it. I shall refer to what I consider to be some of the hazards of this profession, certain of its more satisfying attributes, and a few of the routes that may lead to it. The focus will be on "coping, " which is not to disregard the often creative function of that process.

The word coping means to engage in a contest or combat, successfully, or at least on even terms, or more generally, to overcome problems and difficulties. In the dictionary are listed other meanings: to meet or encounter (archaic) and to come in contact with (obsolete). All of these meanings are applicable to our work. We encounter, and come in contact with, not only the known aspects of our patients, but with distorted and hitherto hidden parts of their personalities; and in turn further revelations of ourselves are produced. Therapy is a journey of meetings, each one different from the other in many respects, and leading to further explorations of which there may seem to be no end. Some of what we do suggests, at times a combat or contest, in that there may be the arousal of anxiety, anger, fear, doubt, a wish to retreat and abandon the field, and a determination to conquer—strange emotions to be associated with what, from one point of view, is thought of as the application of treatment to someone who is sick. More commonly we use the word to denote our meeting with the vicissitudes of existence, and dealing with them adequately to gain some understanding of them, to maintain a degree of separateness and objectivity while involved with them, and to be able to evaluate our own capacities and talents

PSYCHOANALYSTS HAVE LONG BEEN AWARE that in the day to day practice of their somewhat subjective art they can become seduced by their own explanatory constructs. As in any developing discipline there is an intrinsic pressure to accept the empirical success of one's own technique as objective validation for a particular theory of psychological functioning and growth, and refuting those concepts which seem to oppose it. Thus ideational systems become "fact", and "truth" is discovered. Levenson (1972) has developed some general implications of this phenomenon in what he calls "the time-bound nature of psychoanalytic truth". More specifically, a relatively experienced and successful therapist, trying to formulate what he does, must derive his conceptual position, at least in part, from a fundemental need to maintain cognitive consistency.2 His relative dependence upon data coming from within his consulting room fosters the rigidifying of a shared belief system which makes sense of the evidence that his own technique is effective in some consistent way. Committment to a particular version of psychoanalytic "truth" is therefore not only time -bound; it is also bound to the cognitive demand to give structural meaning to the basic dimensions of one's effectiveness at any given point in time while keeping the door open to reconceptualization and change.

James Grotstein  

SUMMARY

It is the contention of this presentation that normal and abnormal personalities evolve from their phantasies of the internal objects comprising them. Normal, neurotic, narcissistic, and perhaps even borderline personalities seem to evolve from a dichotomy of

443

internal objects which are either perverse and/or diabolical on one hand and beneficent and helpful on the other. This dichotomy constitutes the paradigm for all psychic conflict and is essentially a theological one—between good and evil. Schizophrenics, on the contrary, have no confidence in their capacity for boundary formation and therefore form unstable objects of great elasticity which delusionally transform from the violent pressure of abnormal projective identification and abnormal splitting to constitute the paradigm of a psychic defect.

In each case (in the conflict and in the defect) one can see an array of internal objects which appear to be awesome, eerie, controlling, self-serving, and diabolically perverse. They seem to be separate personalities formed by precocious closure within the personality structure. It is my belief further that this internal object paradigm, first described by Klein (1950) and Fairbairn (1954), constitutes the true motivational firing pin of all personalities and should supplant the impulse-drive theory which I believe now to be obsolete. In short, psychopathology is demonology. Finally, I believe that psychic defect may be the demoralized dissembling of a personality altered by a perverse suborganization of great virulence and the analysis of which often reveals an analyzable psychical conflict underneath.

ANNA FREUD'S EFFORT TO GAIN clinical and theoretical perspective in Difficulties in the Path of Psychoanalysis(1969) reaffirmed the view that "the more seriously an individual is torn by conflicts and contradictory forces within himself, the more opportunity he provides for profitable exploration" during the course of analytic treatment (p. 8). Since its inception, psychoanalytic theory has derived primarily from critical questions posed by the often turbulent negativity of intrapsychic conflict and interactional distortion revealed within the framework of the clinical situation. The continuing concern of Freud (1916), (1918), (1923), (1924), (1937), and of numerous other subsequent investigators, with the problem of the "Negative Therapeutic Reaction" (N. T. R.)1 is a prime instance of that process fundamental to the evolution of psychoanalysis whereby serious clinical obstacles become an impetus for reassessment of theory leading to subsequent modifications in practice. The concept of N. T. R. is particularly instructive in this regard since this apparent "inverse" reaction to the progress of the treatment can become "the most powerful of all obstacles to recovery" (Freud, 1923; p. 49), evoking in the analyst a radical questioning of prior theoretical posture and customary technical approach.

PSYCHOANALYTIC LITERATURE OF THE LAST quarter-century reflects two evolutionary developments in the operational concept of countertransference. One is the tempering of the wholly negative attitude it originally evoked, which was so succinctly expressed by Fliess: "undesirable and a hindrance … Ideally, therefore, countertransference should not occur. But it does … always resistance, must always be analyzed" (1953, p. 286). Without disputing the ubiquity of countertransference or dismissing its resistance potential, the theoretical formulations of all psychoanalytic schools currently accord some measure of respect to the phenomenon. In this process of detoxification, outright proscription has given way to thoughtful assessment and specific recommendations for the constructive use of countertransference.

A parallel development, more implicitly suggested in the literature since mid-century, has been the gradual dissolution of the initially monolithic concepts of transference and countertransference. The simultaneity of the so-called widening scope of indications for psychoanalysis and reports of essentially different transference states observed in patients with the more severe emotional disorders was more than coincidental. The existence of narcissistic transference and its implications for the treatment of schizophrenic (Spotnitz, 1969) and non-psychotic patients (Kohut, 1971) were comprehensively explored.

IN THIS PAPER I SHALL APPROACH the subject of countertransference from the point of view of analytical (Jungian) psychology. Since this differs historically and conceptually from classical psychoanalysis I will begin by explicating Jung's position and then consider how his followers have criticized, modified, and developed his point of view. Jung conceived analytic practice to be a dialectical process between two involved persons. By implication he advocated what has lately been called an open systems viewpoint. A closed system is one with clearly defined limits or boundaries. When this obtains there may be two persons related to each other but functioning as two different entities. In their conversation words have an agreed meaning or, if there are dysjunctions in their communications, these can be clarified if necessary by reference to the psychical system of one or the other. Open systems, on the other hand, are those in which boundaries do not have fixed definitions with the result that the two systems interact and change in relation to each other. Difficulties or confusions therefore require a change in both psychical systems before validation is possible.

Developments in psychoanalysis appear to have led psychoanalysts close to conceptions being worked on by analytical psychologists, particularly in London. Robert Langs M.D.

Introduction

IT IS THE ESSENTIAL PURPOSE of this paper1 to develop a reconceptualization of the nature and function of interventions, based upon a study of their effects within the bipersonal field. This presentation will be derived primarily from an adaptational-interactional study of the unconscious communicative interaction between patient and therapist or analyst.2 This approach stands in contrast to existing studies of interventions, which appear to be based upon a classification founded on their manifest properties, rather than on an empirical study of their implications within the therapeutic interaction.

The present study is, then, a distillate derived from extensive clinical observations of the bipersonal field (Langs, 1976a); (1978b), (1978c), and from a recent detailed investigation of the listening process (Langs, 1978d). These efforts have generated a series of empirically derived and validated clinical hypotheses, some of which have related to the analyst's interventions. The present paper extends these initial endeavors by redefining the basic interventions, reconsidering the nature of validation, and studying the indications for, and timing of, the analyst's activities.

The Transference-Countertransference Transaction

Gerard Chrzanowski M.D.

Gerard Chrzanowski

Gerard Chrzanowski, M.D.
250 East 87th Street
New York, N.Y. 10028

Gerard Chrzanowski  

PSYCHOANALYTIC LANGUAGE AND PSYCHOANALYTIC PRACTICE have become increasingly alienated from each other.1 So far we have not succeeded in forging a universally useful set of terms that lends itself to effective clinical application. Every analyst, despite his level of sophistication, is still bound to a host of myths and rituals that tend to get in the way of observational accuracy.

Among the few exceptions to this general problem are the concepts of transference and countertransference. Transference, following anxiety, is the most ubiquitous psychological manifestation. In contrast to many other concepts, transference is a directly observable phenomenon. Every experienced clinician is familiar with a series of overt or covert, intense emotional manifestations that permeate the therapeutic relationship in one form or another. Accordingly, there is no disagreement about the existence of the transference phenomenon per se, inasmuch as transference neither pertains to a structure of the psychic apparatus nor to a metapsychological construct. Sharp differences of opinion occur, however, when it comes to a definition of the basic nature of transference, its particular origin and its clinical implications in the therapeutic process.

It is the thesis of this paper that transference and countertransference constitute a multitide of phenomena that transcend the traditional meaning of the term transference. I view transference and countertransference as reciprocal and interlocking. I believé that the separation of one from the other is not useful clinically.

THE DOCUMENTATION GATHERED ON FREUD now adds up to being the most specific and insightful that we have on any individual in history.1 And yet when Arnold Zweig proposed to write a biography of Freud, he received the resounding answer that "Anyone turning biographer commits himself to lies, to concealment, to hypocrisy, to flattery, and even to hiding his own lack of understanding, for biographical truth is not to be had, and even if it were it couldn't be used."2 As I pored over the immense primary and secondary source material on Freud's life during the 1890's and early 1900's, at every turn I constantly became more and more aware that behind each constellation of enlightening data there were darkened spaces literally as limitless as the unconscious. It is uncontestable that the development of psychoanalysis itself presents some of the most defiant obstacles to psychohistorians. DR. BONIME'S DISCUSSION OF "PARANOID PSYCHODYNAMICS" touches perceptively on a number of central issues in forms of the paranoid psychopathology and provides ample basis for discussion. I will confine the remarks in my discussion to one aspect of his treatment, namely the connection of the dynamics of narcissism with paranoid states, and include some comments on the clinical material he presents.

It should be noted, first of all, that while the concept of paranoid process hovers in the background of the reflections on paranoid psychodynamics, it remains an unfocused and nonspecific background set whose properties never seem to come to bear on or play any significant role in the drama of paranoia. The process note is struck in the first paragraph, but the theme is subsequently abandoned.
